Physical examination reveals a new diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border and a faint, equal radial pulse bilaterally. A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows a dilated aortic root with an intimal flap extending into the ascending aorta. Laboratory studies are pending. 

Given this presentation, outline the immediate management steps, including pharmacologic therapy, imaging priorities, and considerations for transfer to a tertiary center capable of performing emergent surgical repair. Provide concise, evidence‑based recommendations and note any contraindicated interventions.
items.answer:
**Acute Stanford‑type A Aortic Dissection – Immediate ED Management (≤ 1 hour)** | Step | What to do | Why / Evidence | Practical tips | |------|------------|----------------|----------------| | **1. Rapid clinical stabilization** | • **Airway/oxygen** – keep SpO₂ > 94 % (high‑flow O₂ if needed).
• **IV access** – 2 large‑bore (≥14 G) lines; draw labs (CBC, CMP, coag profile, type‑&‑cross, cardiac enzymes, D‑dimer, lactate). | Standard trauma/critical‑care protocol; labs will be needed for surgery. | Keep a “code aortic” sheet handy. | | **2. Immediate analgesia** | • **IV fentanyl** 1–2 µg/kg (repeat q5‑10 min) or **IV morphine** 2–4 mg q5‑10 min until pain < 4/10. | Pain → sympathetic surge → ↑ HR/BP, worsening shear stress. Analgesia alone can drop SBP ≈ 10‑15 mmHg. | Avoid high‑dose sedatives that mask neurologic exam. | | **3. Blood‑pressure & heart‑rate control (first‑line)** | **a. IV β‑blocker** – **Esmolol** 50 µg/kg/min (start → adjust to HR < 60 bpm) or **Labetalol** 20 mg IV bolus (repeat q10 min up to 300 mg).
**b. Once HR ≤ 60 bpm, add a vasodilator** if SBP > 120 mmHg:
• **Nicardipine** 5 mg/h infusion, titrate by 2.5 mg/h q5 min (max 15 mg/h).
• **Clevidipine** 1‑2 mg/h, titrate q2 min (max 21 mg/h). | 2010‑2023 ACC/AHA & ESC guidelines: target SBP 100‑120 mmHg and HR < 60 bpm *as quickly as possible* (within 20 min) to reduce aortic wall stress. β‑blockade *must precede* vasodilators to avoid reflex tachycardia. | • Prepare infusion pumps.
• Continuous arterial line (radial or femoral) for real‑time BP.
• Monitor for bronchospasm (esmolol) or bradycardia. | | **4. Definitive imaging (to confirm type & extent)** | **First‑line** – **Contrast‑enhanced CT angiography (CTA) of chest, abdomen, pelvis** (fast, widely available).
**If CTA unavailable or patient unstable** – **Trans‑esophageal echocardiography (TEE)** at bedside (detects intimal flap, aortic insufficiency, pericardial effusion).
**MRI** – reserved for stable patients when CT/TEE contraindicated. | CTA sensitivity ≈ 98 % for dissection; provides surgical roadmap (involvement of arch, coronary ostia, branch vessels). TEE sensitivity ≈ 95 % and can be done in < 5 min. | • Ensure creatinine is known before contrast; if severe renal dysfunction, go straight to TEE.
• Keep patient supine; avoid neck extension if carotid involvement suspected. | | **5. Initiate emergent surgical pathway** | • **Activate “aortic dissection” code** with cardiothoracic surgery & perfusion services.
• **Arrange immediate transfer** to a tertiary center with on‑site cardiac surgery & hybrid OR (if not already at such a facility).
• **Send blood products** (2 units PRBC, 2 units plasma) & type‑&‑cross.
• **Document** time of symptom onset, vitals, meds given, imaging results. | Type A dissections have > 50 % in‑hospital mortality without surgery; mortality rises ~1–2 % per hour. Early transfer ≤ 6 h improves outcomes. | • Use ground EMS or air‑medical depending on distance (< 1 h flight preferred).
• Provide continuous β‑blocker/vasodilator infusion en route; avoid interruptions. | | **6. Monitor for complications** | • **Continuous ECG, arterial line, pulse oximetry**.
• **Serial neuro exam** (stroke, spinal ischemia).
• **Repeat bedside TTE/TEE** if hemodynamics deteriorate (tamponade, worsening AR). | Acute aortic regurgitation, pericardial tamponade, myocardial ischemia, limb ischemia are emergent surgical modifiers. | • Keep chest tube set ready; pericardiocentesis only if tamponade and surgery delayed (rare). | | **7. Contra‑indicated / to‑avoid interventions** | • **Fibrinolysis** (tPA, streptokinase) – can precipitate fatal hemorrhage.
• **Nitroprusside or nitroglycerin alone** – may cause reflex tachycardia and increase shear stress; only after adequate β‑blockade.
• **High‑dose IV fluids** – can worsen hypertension and aortic wall stress; give only if hypotensive after β‑blockade.
• **Anticoagulation (heparin, DOACs)** – unless there is a compelling indication (e.g., concurrent MI) and surgical team approves; generally avoided. | Recommendations from ACC/AHA 2023 guideline & ESC 2022 consensus. | Document reason if any of these agents are inadvertently given (e.g., patient already on anticoagulation). | --- ### Quick “ED Checklist” (to be read aloud & ticked) 1. **ABC** – secure airway, O₂, 2 large‑bore IVs. 2. **Pain control** – fentanyl 1‑2 µg/kg IV. 3. **β‑blocker** – esmolol infusion (target HR < 60). 4. **Vasodilator** – nicardipine (if SBP > 120 after HR control). 5. **Arterial line** – place, target SBP 100‑120 mmHg. 6. **Imaging** – CTA chest (if stable) **or** bedside TEE. 7. **Activate surgery** – page cardiothoracic, arrange transfer. 8. **Blood products** – type‑&‑cross, send 2 PRBC/2 FFP. 9. **Avoid**: fibrinolysis, nitroprusside alone, unchecked fluids, anticoagulation. 10. **Re‑assess** vitals q5 min, neuro exam q15 min, pain score q10 min. --- ### Transfer Considerations | Item | Details | |------|---------| | **Destination** | Facility with 24/7 cardiac surgery & hybrid OR (e.g., university medical center). | | **Mode** | Air‑medical if > 60 km or > 30 min ground; otherwise ground ambulance with critical‑care crew. | | **En route care** | Continue β‑blocker infusion; titrate nicardipine to maintain SBP 100‑120 mmHg; keep analgesia; monitor arterial line; avoid abrupt BP swings. | | **Documentation** | Transfer sheet: time of symptom onset, BP/HR trends, meds & doses, imaging findings, labs (especially creatinine, CBC, coag), blood product availability, neuro/vascular exam. | | **Legal/Consent** | Obtain informed consent for emergent surgery (if patient alert) or document surrogate decision‑making. | --- **Bottom line:** - **Rapid β‑blockade → controlled vasodilation → analgesia** are the cornerstones before definitive imaging. - **CTA (or TEE if unstable)** confirms a Stanford type A dissection and guides the surgical plan. - **Immediate activation and transfer** to a center capable of emergent open repair (or hybrid arch repair) is mandatory; every minute of delay increases mortality. - **Never give fibrinolysis or vasodilators without β‑blockade**; avoid anticoagulation unless surgically approved. Follow these steps, and the patient’s odds of surviving the acute phase improve dramatically.

items.question:
A 58-year-old woman with a 12‑year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with a 2‑day history of progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and low‑grade fever. She reports recent travel to a coastal region where she participated in a guided snorkeling tour. Her medications include metformin 1000 mg BID, glimepiride 4 mg daily, and a recent addition of a weekly subcutaneous semaglutide injection started 4 weeks ago. On examination, she is tachypneic (RR 28/min), tachycardic (HR 112/min), febrile (38.6 °C), and mildly hypotensive (BP 100/62 mmHg). Oxygen saturation is 88 % on room air, improving to 94 % with 3 L/min nasal cannula. Pulmonary auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds at the right lower lung field with dullness to percussion. Laboratory studies show: WBC 14,800 µL, CRP 12 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.8 ng/mL, serum glucose 210 mg/dL, HbA1c 8.4 %, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m²). A bedside ultrasound demonstrates a right‑sided pleural effusion; thoracentesis yields a cloudy, exudative fluid with pH 7.2, glucose 55 mg/dL, LDH 560 U/L (serum LDH 210 U/L), and neutrophil predominance. Gram stain shows many gram‑positive cocci in chains; culture later grows Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. 

Given this presentation, what is the most appropriate next step in antimicrobial management, taking into account her diabetes, recent GLP‑1 receptor agonist initiation, renal function, and the need for adequate coverage of a complicated parapneumonic effusion? Provide a concise, evidence‑based recommendation, including drug choice, dosing, route, and duration, as well as any necessary adjunctive therapies.
items.answer:
**Recommendation – Empiric treatment of a complicated parapneumonic effusion (empyema) caused by penicillin‑sensitive *Streptococcus pneumoniae*** | Item | Details | |------|---------| | **Antibiotic regimen** | **IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily** **+ IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 h** | | **Rationale** | • *S. pneumoniae* is penicillin‑sensitive, but a third‑generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) provides reliable, high‑dose bactericidal activity and excellent lung‑and‑pleural penetration.
• Complicated parapneumonic effusions are polymicrobial in up to 20 % of cases; anaerobic coverage (metronidazole) is recommended by IDSA/ATS guidelines for empyema.
• Ceftriaxone is cleared hepatically; no dose adjustment needed at eGFR ≈ 68 mL/min/1.73 m².
• Metronidazole is also safe in mild renal impairment (no adjustment needed until eGFR < 30). | | **Alternative** (if β‑lactam allergy) | **IV levofloxacin 750 mg daily** (covers *S. pneumoniae* and many anaerobes) **+ metronidazole 500 mg q8h**. | | **Duration of therapy** | **Total 4–6 weeks** of antimicrobial therapy.
• Minimum **2 weeks of IV** therapy (or until the pleural fluid is sterile and the patient is clinically stable).
• If clinical response is good and the patient can tolerate oral intake, **step‑down to oral amoxicillin‑clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q8h** (or levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily) to complete the course. | | **Adjunctive management** | 1. **Prompt chest‑tube drainage** of the empyema (size‑appropriate tube, preferably 24–28 Fr).
2. **Intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy** (tPA 10 mg + DNase 5 mg daily for up to 3 days) if the fluid is loculated or drainage is inadequate.
3. **Glycemic control** – continue metformin (eGFR > 45) and glimepiride; monitor glucose closely while on steroids (if given) and adjust insulin/ oral agents as needed.
4. **Supportive care** – supplemental O₂ to maintain SpO₂ > 94 %, fluid balance, analgesia, and monitoring for sepsis. | | **Monitoring** | • Daily CBC, CMP, CRP; repeat pleural fluid analysis after 48–72 h of therapy to confirm sterilisation.
• Watch for ceftriaxone‑related biliary sludging or C. difficile; metronidazole side‑effects (neurotoxicity) if prolonged > 2 weeks.
• Renal function: no dose change required but re‑check eGFR weekly. | | **Why semaglutide does not affect the choice** | Semaglutide is a GLP‑1‑RA with no known pharmacokinetic interaction with β‑lactams or metronidazole; it can be continued. | **Bottom line:** Start **IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h**, ensure chest‑tube drainage (with possible intrapleural tPA/DNase), and treat for **4–6 weeks total** (≥2 weeks IV). Adjust to oral step‑down when clinically appropriate. This regimen provides definitive coverage for the identified *S. pneumoniae* and the anaerobic organisms frequently implicated in complicated parapneumonic effusions, while being safe in a diabetic patient with modest renal impairment and recent semaglutide initiation.

items.question: I am a pediatric intensivist at a tertiary care children's hospital in Canada. A 7‑year‑old boy with a known history of Dravet syndrome is admitted after a prolonged convulsive seizure lasting more than 30 minutes despite maximal dosing of intravenous levetiracetam (60 mg/kg bolus) and a continuous infusion of midazolam (0.3 mg/kg/h). The patient is now receiving a second‑line infusion of phenobarbital (3 mg/kg bolus, then 0.5 mg/kg/h) and a loading dose of fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg). His EEG shows ongoing generalized spike‑and‑wave activity, and he remains clinically seizing. His blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg, heart rate 115 bpm, and there is no evidence of organ dysfunction. What evidence‑based rescue medication or therapeutic strategy should be considered next to achieve seizure control, and what are the key dosing and safety considerations for its use in this age group?
items.answer:
**What to try next**

In a child who is already receiving:

* A benzodiazepine infusion (mid‑midazolam 0.3 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹)  
* A barbiturate infusion (phenobarbital 0.5 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹ after a loading dose)  
* A sodium‑channel blocker (fosphenytoin 20 mg PE kg⁻¹)  

the next‑line, evidence‑based rescue strategy for **refractory status epilepticus (RSE)** is a **continuous infusion of an NMDA‑receptor antagonist – intravenous ketamine**.  

Ketamine has the strongest pediatric data among the non‑GABAergic agents and is especially useful when seizures persist despite maximal GABA‑ergic therapy (midazolam + phenobarbital). It also avoids the cardiovascular depression that can be seen with high‑dose propofol or additional barbiturates and is not contraindicated in Dravet syndrome (in fact, it bypasses the sodium‑channel blockade that can aggravate seizures in this disorder).

---

## 1. Ketamine for RSE in children – dosing and administration

| Step | Dose | Rate / Duration | Comments |
|------|------|----------------|----------|
| **Loading dose** | **1 – 2 mg kg⁻¹ IV** (over 1–2 min) | – | Can be given as a single bolus or divided into two 0.5–1 mg kg⁻¹ boluses 1 min apart. |
| **Maintenance infusion** | **5 – 20 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹** (≈0.3 – 1.2 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹) | Titrate up every 5–10 min to clinical/EEG response | Target: burst‑suppression or clear clinical cessation of seizures. |
| **Maximum** | Up to **30 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹** (≈1.8 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹) in severe RSE, but only after careful hemodynamic assessment. | – | Rarely needed in children; most achieve control ≤15 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹. |

*If a rapid bolus is preferred (e.g., when an immediate “stop‑the‑clock” is needed), a **single 2 mg kg⁻¹ bolus** can be given, followed immediately by the infusion.*  

**Weight‑based calculations for a 7‑year‑old (≈30 kg):**  

* Loading: 30–60 mg IV (1–2 mg kg⁻¹).  
* Maintenance start: 150–600 µg min⁻¹ (≈0.9–3.6 mg h⁻¹).  

---

## 2. Safety and monitoring considerations

| Issue | What to watch for | Practical mitigation |
|-------|-------------------|----------------------|
| **Cardiovascular** | Transient hypertension & tachycardia (common); rare hypotension at high doses. | Continuous arterial BP or non‑invasive beat‑to‑beat monitoring; treat hypertension with short‑acting agents (e.g., nicardipine) if MAP > 110 mm Hg. |
| **Intracranial pressure (ICP)** | Ketamine can raise ICP in patients with impaired autoregulation. | Ensure adequate sedation and ventilation; consider concurrent hyperventilation or osmotherapy if ICP is a concern. |
| **Respiratory** | Loss of airway reflexes → need for endotracheal intubation. | The patient is already intubated for midazolam/phenobarbital infusions; continue ventilatory support and monitor end‑tidal CO₂. |
| **Neuro‑psychiatric / emergence phenomena** | Hallucinations, vivid dreams, dysphoria on awakening. | Give a short benzodiazepine “cover” (e.g., lorazepam 0.05 mg kg⁻¹) before discontinuation; use a slow wean. |
| **Renal / Hepatic** | Ketamine is metabolised hepatically; active metabolite norketamine is renally excreted. | No dose adjustment needed in normal liver/renal function; monitor urine output and liver enzymes if infusion > 24 h. |
| **Seizure recurrence on wean** | “Rebound” seizures when ketamine is tapered too quickly. | Taper slowly (e.g., reduce by 10–20 % per 6 h) while watching EEG; maintain at least one other AED at therapeutic level (e.g., phenobarbital). |
| **Drug interactions** | Additive CNS depression with phenobarbital and midazolam. | Keep total sedation scores in target range (RASS –3 to –4). Adjust benzodiazepine infusion downward as ketamine dose rises. |

**Laboratory monitoring**

* Baseline and q6‑h electrolytes, glucose, liver enzymes, and renal function.  
* Serum ketamine levels are not routinely measured, but if prolonged infusion (> 48 h) consider checking for accumulation.  
* Continuous EEG (cEEG) is mandatory to confirm electrographic seizure control and to guide weaning.

---

## 3. Why ketamine is preferred over other “third‑line” options in this scenario

| Option | Pros | Cons in this patient |
|--------|------|----------------------|
| **Propofol infusion** (2–5 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹) | Rapid onset, good EEG control | **Propofol infusion syndrome** (especially > 48 h, high dose); risk of severe hypotension; already on high‑dose barbiturates → additive depression. |
| **Pentobarbital/thiopental coma** | Powerful GABA‑ergic suppression | Profound hypotension, need for massive vasoactive support; already on phenobarbital; risk of oversedation and prolonged ventilation. |
| **Inhalational anesthetic (isoflurane, sevoflurane)** | Excellent seizure suppression, easy titration | Requires specialized delivery system, can increase ICP, may cause malignant hyperthermia; logistics in a pediatric ICU are more complex. |
| **Additional sodium‑channel blocker (e.g., lacosamide)** | Good adjunctive efficacy | Dravet syndrome patients are **sodium‑channel‑sensitive**; further blockade can worsen seizures. |
| **IV valproic acid** (20–40 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹) | Broad‑spectrum AED, works in RSE | Hepatotoxicity risk, especially with concomitant phenobarbital; limited data in children < 2 y (our patient is older, but cumulative hepatotoxic load already high). |
| **Ketamine** | NMDA antagonism works when GABA‑ergic drugs have failed; preserves blood pressure; minimal hepatic metabolism at usual pediatric doses; growing pediatric RSE literature (e.g., 2021‑2024 systematic reviews show > 70 % seizure termination). | Needs airway protection (already in place); monitor for hypertension/ICP. |

Because the child is already **intubated, hemodynamically stable, and has no organ dysfunction**, ketamine offers the best risk‑benefit profile.

---

## 4. Practical “step‑by‑step” plan for the bedside team

1. **Confirm that the patient is fully protected** (endotracheal tube, cuff inflated, adequate ventilation, sedation score ≤ ‑3).  
2. **Obtain baseline labs** (CBC, BMP, LFTs, coagulation).  
3. **Administer ketamine loading dose**: 1 mg kg⁻¹ IV over 1 min (e.g., 30 mg for a 30‑kg child).  
4. **Start continuous infusion** at 10 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹ (≈0.6 mg kg⁻¹ h⁻¹).  
5. **Re‑assess EEG and clinical status** after 5–10 min; if seizures persist, increase by 5 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹ every 5 min up to a maximum of 20–30 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹.  
6. **Titrate down the midazolam infusion** as ketamine takes effect (avoid excessive sedation).  
7. **Maintain cEEG** for at least 24 h after seizure cessation; aim for burst‑suppression or clear background.  
8. **Wean ketamine** once a stable EEG pattern is achieved and other AEDs are at therapeutic levels: reduce infusion by 10–20 % every 6 h, monitoring for rebound.  
9. **Document and communicate** the plan with the multidisciplinary team (neurology, pharmacy, nursing, respiratory therapists).  

---

## 5. Key take‑home points for the pediatric intensivist

* **Ketamine infusion (5–20 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹ after a 1–2 mg kg⁻¹ loading dose)** is the next evidence‑based rescue medication for a child with RSE after failure of benzodiazepine, phenobarbital, and fosphenytoin.  
* It is **hemodynamically favorable**, does **not rely on GABA‑ergic mechanisms**, and is **not contraindicated in Dravet syndrome**.  
* **Safety monitoring**: continuous BP, heart rate, ICP (if relevant), EEG, and routine labs; be prepared to treat hypertension or manage potential ICP rise.  
* **Airway protection** is mandatory; the patient is already intubated, making ketamine safe to use.  
* Once seizures are controlled, **gradual weaning** of ketamine while maintaining at least one other AED (phenobarbital or levetiracetam) will minimise rebound seizures.  

If ketamine fails to achieve electrographic control after an adequate trial (≥ 30 min at the maximal tolerated infusion), the next escalation would be a **barbiturate coma (pentobarbital) or an inhalational anesthetic (isoflurane)**, but these carry significantly higher cardiovascular and metabolic risks and should be reserved for truly refractory cases.  

---  

**Bottom line:** Initiate an IV ketamine loading dose (1–2 mg kg⁻¹) followed by a continuous infusion titrated to 5–20 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹, with vigilant hemodynamic, respiratory, and EEG monitoring, as the next evidence‑based rescue strategy for this 7‑year‑old with Dravet‑related refractory status epilepticus.
